Child geniuses

By: Eugene Botha | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
……meet a few of South Africa’s young geniuses

Unique Selling Point:
South Africa is not all bad news -- there are also amazing people in the country. We look at a few exceptional children.

Summary:
We all know something about geniuses. People like Einstein or Mozart or Stephen Hawking. And we see child prodigies on television sometimes. But geniuses are not only found in far-off overseas countries. There are also geniuses walking among us, and some of them are very, very young and found in the most unexpected places. In this segment we are looking at a few of South Africa’s child geniuses.

Further information:
We all know something about geniuses. People like Einstein or Mozart or Stephen Hawking. And we see child prodigies on television sometimes. But geniuses are not only found in far-off overseas countries. There are also geniuses walking among us, and some of them are very, very young and found in the most unexpected places. In this segment we are looking at a few of South Africa’s child geniuses.

1. Take for example Sibahle Zwane (mother Mbali Zwane 072 616 4972). He is a young math genius that was discovered by accident by a passer-by.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IFHckSOh5r0. This video of Sibahle spitting out sums like rhymes has gone viral on social media in 11 months ago. He is now 10 and in grade 4. His mum Mbali Zwane said her son has a special gift and is the star of the family. “Sibahle has been good with numbers since he was four,” she said. “Even when he’s playing with friends, he comes up with answers to hard questions. His teachers always tell me he’s a maths genius.” Mbali said if her son had maths books he would be the smartest boy in his school. “He has no books, but he has always written numbers on the wall. His interest in maths has always been obvious.” Mbali said the child doesn’t do the calculations manually but sees the numbers in his mind. He is genius lies in multiplication of high numbers. He is less adept at addition and subtraction. Mbali and her son Sibahle lives with Mbali’s father who gets an old age pension. They all live off his pension and are very poor. Mbali does not have work at the moment. They live in Lehae, South of Joburg, apparently near Lenasia, and they are willing to speak to us.

2. Then there is Grade 10 learner Farida Cajee at Hoërskool Schweizer Reneke, who won a gold medal and the Eskom Special Award for Best Female Development Project at the Dr Ruth Segomotsi Mompati District Expo. She has developed a 3D printed hand that is also mind-controlled. She wrote a computer programme and linked it to and EEG cap that enables the wearer to control a robotic hand by just thinking. The wearer can even control individual finger. Such hands already exist and Carte Blanche has done stories on such hands, but those hands cost millions of dollars. This is a cheap and effective alternative developed in South Africa. Farida’s father is a motor mechanic and her mother a housewife. Fificajee@icloud.com, tel no 0646520684.

3. Nine-year-old Stiaan Scheepers, from Rustenburg, flew the flag high when he came second at the Junior Mental Calculation World Championship, which took place in Germany this week. His victory is made sweeter by the fact this little fighter is a Leukaemia survivor. His mother Elmarie, bursting with pride and wonder at her son's amazing skill, explained that when Stiaan was two, his father Louis died very suddenly at the age of 42 due to complications following a medical condition. But before his father died, he suggested to Elmarie that they start finding a place to prepare Stiaan's brother, who was six at the time, for the very high expectations that schools have in terms of mathematics. The maths preparation school they settled on, called A+ Students, was a very long drive away. When Elmarie happened to mention in passing over the phone that she would be driving with a toddler, they invited her to let Stiaan join the classes too because they start the children off young. He was just two years and three months old when he started at the school, which uses the Japanese abacus method of mastering numbers and calculations. Andy Raouna, CEO of A+ Students, explained that they use the Japanese abacus called a Soroban, which combines play and sensory learning. The children start understanding the concept of numbers with the abacus, then are weaned off it to do mental calculations. He says this is why a person who was taught numbers using an abacus can sometimes be seen tapping their fingers almost absently as they ponder the calculation in front them. "In their mind they are moving beads, that's why their fingers move," he explained. "We've lost the ability to do mental calculations, and a lot of people haven't learnt it in the first place," said Raouna, who is also the director of PAMA SA, the local branch of the Pan Pacific Abacus & Mental Arithmetic Association.

4. While most 14-year-olds are still juniors in high school, gifted 14-year-old Hjalmar Rall starts his university career at Pretoria University on Friday. Hjalmar, from Riebeek Kasteel in the Western Cape, is starting his first year of a B.Sc in physics. Hjalmar’s father, Heinrich, says his son started with orientation this week and will start attending lectures on Monday. Since the university placed a report on Hjalmar on its website on Monday his family, who have moved to Pretoria, have been overwhelmed by the media. Hjalmar’s dad says he wanted to be close to his minor son to support him in his new adventure. Read more: What does a university education in SA cost right now? “At this stage we want to protect him and give him the opportunity to find his feet. He’s looking forward to it.” Last year Hjalmar obtained his A Levels through Cambridge International Exams, the equivalent of matric, by means of home schooling. On a single day he wrote the physics, chemistry and maths exams. Pretoria University reports that Hjalmar chose the university because he believed it was “the best university”. Hjalmar, who finds challenges motivating, says he does not have a secret formula to success but strongly believes that when you enjoy doing something you’re bound to succeed. He believes success lies in doing fun things. “As long as it's not boring, I do it,” he says. He wants to discover a world that no one has ever discovered before. “I want to ask even bigger questions and find out what else there is to do, particularly in theoretical physics and astrophysics.”

5. Expert. Mrs. Riana de Villiers. Educational Psychologist specialising in Gifted children
083 448 7420, riana.devilliers@mensa.org.za

Treatment to be discussed in full. We will explore the gifts of the various children and tell their personal stories – let Sibahle do multiplication, let Stiaan tell us on what day of the week a few dates are, let Farida demonstrate her robotic hand and let’s talk to 15 year old Hjalmar about his second year at University. We will use Riana de Villiers as expert to help us understand giftedness and genius a little better – also the particular challenges gifted children face in education and the world.

Press Release:


Child Geniuses
They’re rare, highly intelligent and often years ahead of their age. Child geniuses are not only an overseas phenomenon – South Africa has a number of exceptional young minds. From an extraordinary 10 year-old mathematician to a 14 year-old scientist on the cusp of technological development – these children are competing with adults at the highest levels. Carte Blanche meets these brilliant prodigies.
Producer: Eugene Botha
Presenter: Derek Watts


Script:


V/O:
If you hear the word “genius” what comes to mind?

Surely Da Vinci qualifies….

And Einstein of course….

And perhaps somebody like Steven Hawking.

LINK:
But geniuses are not only found in far flung lands. We’ve got our own crop here in South Africa. And they come in surprisingly small packages.

V/O:
We took a road trip in search of these exceptional minds that belong to young children. Many of their skills have attracted national attention, but that is not all.

LINK:
Some of our budding geniuses have even showcased their talents on the world stage.

V/O:
We found one of them in Rustenburg. Nine-year-old Stiaan Scheepers has an extraordinary mathematics talent and has been competing in the Junior Mental Calculation World Championship for a number of years. This year, he came second in the world. One of the skills he has is to calculate within seconds on which day of the week a certain date fell.
Derek:
Stiaan, we’ve got a special date here. July 18, 1918. Nelson Mandela, Madiba’s birthday. What day of the week was it?
Stiaan:
Thursday
Derek:
Thursday is correct
V/O:
Stiaan is making the movements with his fingers because he has been taught how to do mental calculations in a Japanese system that teaches mathematics with a Soroban or abacus. This enables children to do rapid mental calculations.

Stiaan’s mother Elmarie says Stiaan is a cancer survivor and he also lost his father when he was 7. But despite this he excels in mental calculations and has competed all over the world, against the best in the world, and won.

Before we left we gave Stiaan a really tough test.
Derek:
764392 x 427656, and away you go!
Stiaan:
Wow, I am done.
Derek:
Just check and call the numbers out to me.
764392 x 427656
So, let’s see if you are right. Call out your answer.
Stiaan:
326 896 825 152
Derek:
Well done, Stiaan, well done!
V/O:
From Rustenburg we continued our quest.
LINK:
Some of our genius kids want to make a difference in the world, and a grade ten learner from Schweizer-Reneke is a good example.
V/O:
Her name is Farida Cajee, a serial inventor and high achiever at the Escom Expo for Young Scientists. She has won many regional and national awards for her inventions.
Derek:
Tell us about some of your projects.
Farida:
2015 was the first time I was chosen to represent the region at the internationals is Boksburg. For that I did banana bio-plastic. So I used banana peels and developed a bio=degradable type of plastic that can be made into , to wrap chords, or even a checkers plastic recycling bags.
V/O:
This year she won a gold and a bunch of other awards with something extraordinary. Touched by the fate of war zone amputees, she invented a mind controlled 3d printed prosthetic hand. She had parts of a hand 3D printed elsewhere and then combined it with a regular EEG headset that can read brainwaves. She tweaked the various components, used a drone sensor and cell phone app, and created a hand that moves when you concentrate hard enough.

I also tried the headset and concentrated and indeed, I got the fingers to move.

Derek:
Where do you get this inventive streak from?
Farida:
I am a basic girl with a complex brain
Derek:
With a complex brain!
V/O:
We bid the girl with the complex brain farewell and took to the road again.

Radford House is a school for gifted children in Johannesburg. Philip Kokot is the headmaster and says giftedness is not celebrated enough in our school system.
Philip:
The reality is that gifted children have very unique characteristics and needs. They learn differently, they interact with knowledge differently, they interact with people differently, and when not understood and not accommodated, not only can they lose confidence and motivation, but also they can underachieve, they can pose that spark, they can hide away from the world. And the end of it all, the world needs them. We don’t need people who can churn out facts, but we do need people who can come up with new solutions. People who are born problem solvers. People who are designed to change the world for the better and that’s gifted adults and gifted adults are not being produced at the level they could be because they are being lost at the child phase, mainly due to the education system not recognizing that they are a reality.
V/O:
Our journey taught us a lot about gifted children.
LINK:
What we found is that genius is everywhere like here in the streets of Lehae, South of Soweto.
V/O:
This is where 10-year-old Sibahle Zwane lives. His mathematical abilities astounded people around the country last year.

It all started with this incidental video that went viral. In the video a motorist films Sibahle’s amazing ability to do complex mental multiplication virtually instantly.
UP SOUND
Derek:
Do you remember talking to a motorist who took a video and that made you famous.
Sibahle
I greeted him and he asked about maths. I answered him and he gave me R7.
V/O:
We decided to put Sibahle to the test ourselves.
Derek:
So, lets, and I am using the calculator cause my maths is bad. Let’s do 892 x 650
Sibahle:
579 800
Derek:
Spot on! Well done!
What do you want to be when you grow up?
Sibahle:
I want to be a pilot. I want to fly.
Derek:
You are already flying with your maths.
V/O:
Since Sibahle appeared on-line a private school has offered him a bursary for next year and also offered his mother a job at the school.

We said our goodbyes and continued our journey.
V/O:
When some exceptional young minds are recognized early on and developed, they can become extraordinary academic achievers. On the campus of the University of Pretoria we caught up with second year student Hjalmar Rall.
Hjalmar:
I just turned sixteen and I have been studying physics at UP now for two years. I started at the beginning of 2017 and I had just turned fourteen.
V/O:
This is what he looked like on his first day of University. He is the youngest person ever to be admitted to the institution.
Hjalmar:
I still looked like a little kid then. A lot of people asked me about myself and a lot of people being very impressed, but it sort of petered out after a while, and most people accept me as a student now.
V/O:
Hjalmar is often asked why he decided on a degree in physics.
Hjalmar:
I am not quite sure, I think I might have gone into mathematics, but physics – you get to play with mathematics get to ask big questions but more juts play with mathematics. That was the big thing.
V/O:
Hjalmar was home schooled from Grade 5 and advanced so rapidly that he qualified for University admittance at the tender age of 14, and and just keeps on excelling.
Hjalmar:
I still looked like a little kid then. There was a lot of people asking me about myself, and a lot of people being really impressed, but it sort of petered out after a while, and most people accept me as a student now.
V/O:
Hjalmar is often asked why he decided on a degree in physics.
Hjalmar:
I am not quite sure. I think I might have gone into mathematics for the challenge but in physics you get to play with mathematics. You get to ask big questions but more just play with mathematics.

V/O
Hjalmar’s academic career is blossoming and he is set to graduate with a BSc degree next year.
Philip Kokot says that gifted children should be recognized and celebrated and given room to develop their own unique talents.

Philip:
We all know that everything, the camera in front of us, the technology around it. Every aspect of our life is made better by that child who perhaps did not fit in well at school, who saw things a little differently. There is a lovely quote by Schopenhauer who said that talent is hitting a target that no one else can hit, but genius is hitting a target that no one else has seen. And that is the essence of giftedness and that is the part that we really need to celebrate.

Stiaan: Thursday Derek: Thursday is correct V/O: Stiaan is making the movements with his fingers because he has been taught how to do mental calculations in a Japanese system that teaches mathematics with a Soroban or abacus. This enables children to do rapid mental calculations. Stiaan’s mother Elmarie says Stiaan is a cancer survivor and he also lost his father when he was 7. But despite this he excels in mental calculations and has competed all over the world, against the best in the world, and won. Before we left we gave Stiaan a really tough test. Derek: 764392 x 427656, and away you go! Stiaan: Wow, I am done. Derek: Just check and call the numbers out to me. 764392 x 427656 So, let’s see if you are right. Call out your answer. Stiaan: 326 896 825 152 Derek: Well done, Stiaan, well done! V/O: From Rustenburg we continued our quest. LINK: Some of our genius kids want to make a difference in the world, and a grade ten learner from Schweizer-Reneke is a good example. V/O: Her name is Farida Cajee, a serial inventor and high achiever at the Escom Expo for Young Scientists. She has won many regional and national awards for her inventions. Derek: Tell us about some of your projects. Farida: 2015 was the first time I was chosen to represent the region at the internationals is Boksburg. For that I did banana bio-plastic. So I used banana peels and developed a bio=degradable type of plastic that can be made into , to wrap chords, or even a checkers plastic recycling bags. V/O: This year she won a gold and a bunch of other awards with something extraordinary. Touched by the fate of war zone amputees, she invented a mind controlled 3d printed prosthetic hand. She had parts of a hand 3D printed elsewhere and then combined it with a regular EEG headset that can read brainwaves. She tweaked the various components, used a drone sensor and cell phone app, and created a hand that moves when you concentrate hard enough. I also tried the headset and concentrated and indeed, I got the fingers to move. Derek: Where do you get this inventive streak from? Farida: I am a basic girl with a complex brain Derek: With a complex brain! V/O: We bid the girl with the complex brain farewell and took to the road again. Radford House is a school for gifted children in Johannesburg. Philip Kokot is the headmaster and says giftedness is not celebrated enough in our school system. Philip: The reality is that gifted children have very unique characteristics and needs. They learn differently, they interact with knowledge differently, they interact with people differently, and when not understood and not accommodated, not only can they lose confidence and motivation, but also they can underachieve, they can pose that spark, they can hide away from the world. And the end of it all, the world needs them. We don’t need people who can churn out facts, but we do need people who can come up with new solutions. People who are born problem solvers. People who are designed to change the world for the better and that’s gifted adults and gifted adults are not being produced at the level they could be because they are being lost at the child phase, mainly due to the education system not recognizing that they are a reality. V/O: Our journey taught us a lot about gifted children. LINK: What we found is that genius is everywhere like here in the streets of Lehae, South of Soweto. V/O: This is where 10-year-old Sibahle Zwane lives. His mathematical abilities astounded people around the country last year. It all started with this incidental video that went viral. In the video a motorist films Sibahle’s amazing ability to do complex mental multiplication virtually instantly. UP SOUND Derek: Do you remember talking to a motorist who took a video and that made you famous. Sibahle I greeted him and he asked about maths. I answered him and he gave me R7. V/O: We decided to put Sibahle to the test ourselves. Derek: So, lets, and I am using the calculator cause my maths is bad. Let’s do 892 x 650 Sibahle: 579 800 Derek: Spot on! Well done! What do you want to be when you grow up? Sibahle: I want to be a pilot. I want to fly. Derek: You are already flying with your maths. V/O: Since Sibahle appeared on-line a private school has offered him a bursary for next year and also offered his mother a job at the school. We said our goodbyes and continued our journey. V/O: When some exceptional young minds are recognized early on and developed, they can become extraordinary academic achievers. On the campus of the University of Pretoria we caught up with second year student Hjalmar Rall. Hjalmar: I just turned sixteen and I have been studying physics at UP now for two years. I started at the beginning of 2017 and I had just turned fourteen. V/O: This is what he looked like on his first day of University. He is the youngest person ever to be admitted to the institution. Hjalmar: I still looked like a little kid then. A lot of people asked me about myself and a lot of people being very impressed, but it sort of petered out after a while, and most people accept me as a student now. V/O: Hjalmar is often asked why he decided on a degree in physics. Hjalmar: I am not quite sure, I think I might have gone into mathematics, but physics – you get to play with mathematics get to ask big questions but more juts play with mathematics. That was the big thing. V/O: Hjalmar was home schooled from Grade 5 and advanced so rapidly that he qualified for University admittance at the tender age of 14, and and just keeps on excelling. Hjalmar: I still looked like a little kid then. There was a lot of people asking me about myself, and a lot of people being really impressed, but it sort of petered out after a while, and most people accept me as a student now. V/O: Hjalmar is often asked why he decided on a degree in physics. Hjalmar: I am not quite sure. I think I might have gone into mathematics for the challenge but in physics you get to play with mathematics. You get to ask big questions but more just play with mathematics. V/O Hjalmar’s academic career is blossoming and he is set to graduate with a BSc degree next year. Philip Kokot says that gifted children should be recognized and celebrated and given room to develop their own unique talents. Philip: We all know that everything, the camera in front of us, the technology around it. Every aspect of our life is made better by that child who perhaps did not fit in well at school, who saw things a little differently. There is a lovely quote by Schopenhauer who said that talent is hitting a target that no one else can hit, but genius is hitting a target that no one else has seen. And that is the essence of giftedness and that is the part that we really need to celebrate.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ……meet a few of South Africa’s young geniuses
metadata.Unique Selling Point: South Africa is not all bad news -- there are also amazing people in the country. We look at a few exceptional children.
metadata.Summary: We all know something about geniuses. People like Einstein or Mozart or Stephen Hawking. And we see child prodigies on television sometimes. But geniuses are not only found in far-off overseas countries. There are also geniuses walking among us, and some of them are very, very young and found in the most unexpected places. In this segment we are looking at a few of South Africa’s child geniuses.
metadata.Further information: We all know something about geniuses. People like Einstein or Mozart or Stephen Hawking. And we see child prodigies on television sometimes. But geniuses are not only found in far-off overseas countries. There are also geniuses walking among us, and some of them are very, very young and found in the most unexpected places. In this segment we are looking at a few of South Africa’s child geniuses. 1. Take for example Sibahle Zwane (mother Mbali Zwane 072 616 4972). He is a young math genius that was discovered by accident by a passer-by. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IFHckSOh5r0. This video of Sibahle spitting out sums like rhymes has gone viral on social media in 11 months ago. He is now 10 and in grade 4. His mum Mbali Zwane said her son has a special gift and is the star of the family. “Sibahle has been good with numbers since he was four,” she said. “Even when he’s playing with friends, he comes up with answers to hard questions. His teachers always tell me he’s a maths genius.” Mbali said if her son had maths books he would be the smartest boy in his school. “He has no books, but he has always written numbers on the wall. His interest in maths has always been obvious.” Mbali said the child doesn’t do the calculations manually but sees the numbers in his mind. He is genius lies in multiplication of high numbers. He is less adept at addition and subtraction. Mbali and her son Sibahle lives with Mbali’s father who gets an old age pension. They all live off his pension and are very poor. Mbali does not have work at the moment. They live in Lehae, South of Joburg, apparently near Lenasia, and they are willing to speak to us. 2. Then there is Grade 10 learner Farida Cajee at Hoërskool Schweizer Reneke, who won a gold medal and the Eskom Special Award for Best Female Development Project at the Dr Ruth Segomotsi Mompati District Expo. She has developed a 3D printed hand that is also mind-controlled. She wrote a computer programme and linked it to and EEG cap that enables the wearer to control a robotic hand by just thinking. The wearer can even control individual finger. Such hands already exist and Carte Blanche has done stories on such hands, but those hands cost millions of dollars. This is a cheap and effective alternative developed in South Africa. Farida’s father is a motor mechanic and her mother a housewife. Fificajee@icloud.com, tel no 0646520684. 3. Nine-year-old Stiaan Scheepers, from Rustenburg, flew the flag high when he came second at the Junior Mental Calculation World Championship, which took place in Germany this week. His victory is made sweeter by the fact this little fighter is a Leukaemia survivor. His mother Elmarie, bursting with pride and wonder at her son's amazing skill, explained that when Stiaan was two, his father Louis died very suddenly at the age of 42 due to complications following a medical condition. But before his father died, he suggested to Elmarie that they start finding a place to prepare Stiaan's brother, who was six at the time, for the very high expectations that schools have in terms of mathematics. The maths preparation school they settled on, called A+ Students, was a very long drive away. When Elmarie happened to mention in passing over the phone that she would be driving with a toddler, they invited her to let Stiaan join the classes too because they start the children off young. He was just two years and three months old when he started at the school, which uses the Japanese abacus method of mastering numbers and calculations. Andy Raouna, CEO of A+ Students, explained that they use the Japanese abacus called a Soroban, which combines play and sensory learning. The children start understanding the concept of numbers with the abacus, then are weaned off it to do mental calculations. He says this is why a person who was taught numbers using an abacus can sometimes be seen tapping their fingers almost absently as they ponder the calculation in front them. "In their mind they are moving beads, that's why their fingers move," he explained. "We've lost the ability to do mental calculations, and a lot of people haven't learnt it in the first place," said Raouna, who is also the director of PAMA SA, the local branch of the Pan Pacific Abacus & Mental Arithmetic Association. 4. While most 14-year-olds are still juniors in high school, gifted 14-year-old Hjalmar Rall starts his university career at Pretoria University on Friday. Hjalmar, from Riebeek Kasteel in the Western Cape, is starting his first year of a B.Sc in physics. Hjalmar’s father, Heinrich, says his son started with orientation this week and will start attending lectures on Monday. Since the university placed a report on Hjalmar on its website on Monday his family, who have moved to Pretoria, have been overwhelmed by the media. Hjalmar’s dad says he wanted to be close to his minor son to support him in his new adventure. Read more: What does a university education in SA cost right now? “At this stage we want to protect him and give him the opportunity to find his feet. He’s looking forward to it.” Last year Hjalmar obtained his A Levels through Cambridge International Exams, the equivalent of matric, by means of home schooling. On a single day he wrote the physics, chemistry and maths exams. Pretoria University reports that Hjalmar chose the university because he believed it was “the best university”. Hjalmar, who finds challenges motivating, says he does not have a secret formula to success but strongly believes that when you enjoy doing something you’re bound to succeed. He believes success lies in doing fun things. “As long as it's not boring, I do it,” he says. He wants to discover a world that no one has ever discovered before. “I want to ask even bigger questions and find out what else there is to do, particularly in theoretical physics and astrophysics.” 5. Expert. Mrs. Riana de Villiers. Educational Psychologist specialising in Gifted children 083 448 7420, riana.devilliers@mensa.org.za Treatment to be discussed in full. We will explore the gifts of the various children and tell their personal stories – let Sibahle do multiplication, let Stiaan tell us on what day of the week a few dates are, let Farida demonstrate her robotic hand and let’s talk to 15 year old Hjalmar about his second year at University. We will use Riana de Villiers as expert to help us understand giftedness and genius a little better – also the particular challenges gifted children face in education and the world.
